title: Keeping the Kitchen Clean
summary: Daily, weekly and monthly kitchen routines; the difference between cleaning and sanitizing; how to use bleach safely; and how to care for dishcloths, sponges, the fridge, oven, microwave, dishwasher, sink and drains, with tips to keep pests out.

list: Wash dishes, or run and empty the dishwasher.
Wipe counters, the stove top and the table with hot, soapy water.
Sanitize any surface raw meat, poultry or their juices touched.
Wipe spills in the fridge and microwave as they happen.
Hang dishcloths to dry; swap in a clean one if it smells or after raw-meat cleanup.
Sweep up crumbs and take out full trash.
Check the fridge for old leftovers and toss anything past its time.
Wash dishcloths and towels in the hot cycle.
Run sponges through the dishwasher with a drying cycle, or replace them.
Wipe the microwave inside, the small appliances, the cabinet fronts and the handles.
Clean the sink and sanitize it after raw meat.
Mop the floor.
Empty and wipe out the fridge with warm water and baking soda.
Clean the dishwasher’s removable parts and wipe the inside.
Clean the oven when it needs it, following its manual.
Oil wooden boards and spoons.
Check the pantry: wipe shelves, look for pests, use older food first.
Check under the sink for leaks.

p: A printable checklist is on the [printables page](/meal-prep/kitchen/print/#k-clean).
These words mean different things, and the order matters: clean first, then sanitize.
list: **Cleaning** “removes most germs, dirt, and impurities from surfaces.” You clean with water, soap and scrubbing. This is most of what a kitchen needs.
**Sanitizing** “reduces germs to levels public health codes or regulations consider safe.” Use it on surfaces that touched raw meat, poultry or their juices.
**Disinfecting** “kills most germs on surfaces and objects.” It is for when someone in the house is sick, more than for everyday cooking.
sections.tip: Let sanitized items air-dry. The CDC says not to rub or pat them with a dish towel, which can put germs back.

p: Bleach works well, but it must be mixed correctly and used alone. **First, read the label on your bottle and follow it.** If the bottle gives no directions, these are the CDC’s:

> For food-contact surfaces such as countertops and plates: “Sanitize in a solution of 1 tablespoon of household chlorine bleach in 1 gallon of clean water.” (CDC, *How to Safely Clean and Sanitize with Bleach*)

> For disinfecting: “5 tablespoons (1/3 cup) of bleach per gallon of room temperature water” or “4 teaspoons of bleach per quart of room temperature water.” Leave it on for at least 1 minute, and make a fresh batch each day. (CDC, *Cleaning and Disinfecting with Bleach*)

The CDC says to use regular, unscented household bleach with 5% to 9% sodium hypochlorite, clean visible dirt off first, and open a window or run a fan. USDA’s *Kitchen Companion* gives the same 1 tablespoon per gallon for cutting boards.
sections.warn: **Never mix bleach with ammonia, with acids such as vinegar, or with any other cleaner.** Bleach and ammonia make toxic chloramine gas. Bleach and acids (vinegar, some toilet-bowl and drain cleaners, rust removers) make chlorine gas. Use one product at a time, and store all cleaners out of reach of children and pets.

list: Damp cloths and sponges are where kitchen germs like to live, and they spread them to every surface they wipe.
Wash dishcloths often in the hot cycle of the washing machine. Keep a stack so you can grab a clean one.
In a USDA study, sponges run through a dishwasher with a drying cycle lost 99.9998% of their bacteria. Soaking sponges in a weak bleach solution or lemon juice worked far less well.
Replace sponges when they smell, fall apart, or stay slimy after cleaning.
Keep it at **40°F or below** and the freezer at **0°F or below**. A separate appliance thermometer tells you for sure; the built-in dial does not.
Wipe up spills right away, especially drips from raw meat, poultry and fish.
Once a week, look for leftovers and food past its date.

For a deep clean, take the food out and wipe the inside, drawers and door seal with **2 teaspoons of baking soda in a quart of warm water**. Skip strong soaps and harsh chemicals, which can leave smells.
An open box of baking soda on a shelf helps with odors.
Let the oven cool completely first.
Wash the inside with warm, soapy water, then rinse so no soap is left. Soak the racks in the sink.
If your oven has a self-clean setting, follow the manual for it, and keep the room aired out.
Wipe the stove top after each meal once it’s cool, so spills don’t bake on.
Wipe up spatters and spills when they happen, so they don’t harden.
For stuck spots, use a paste of baking soda and water, or mild dish soap.
Don’t use oven cleaner or steel wool inside a microwave.
Throw out food scraps that collect in the bottom.
Wash the removable parts (most have a filter that lifts out) in the sink with warm, soapy water.
Wipe the inside and the door edges. Your manual says how often to clean the filter for your model.
Wash the sink with hot, soapy water. Sanitize it after it has held raw meat or poultry, or the water used to clean them.
Keep grease, fats and harsh chemicals out of the drain. Let grease cool and harden, then scrape it into the trash.
Never mix a drain cleaner with bleach or any other cleaner.
Fix a dripping faucet or a leak under the sink; standing water draws pests.

p: Cross-contamination is when germs from raw meat, poultry, seafood or eggs get onto food that won’t be cooked, like salad or bread.
list: Keep one board for produce and ready-to-eat food, and another for raw meat, poultry and seafood. Different colors help.
Wash boards in hot, soapy water after each use. Sanitize after raw meat with 1 tablespoon of unscented liquid chlorine bleach in 1 gallon of water, then rinse and let air-dry.
Wash knives, tongs and plates that touched raw meat before using them for cooked food.
Replace boards that are badly worn or have deep grooves.

p: These steps are about prevention: keep food, water and hiding places away from pests.
list: Store open food such as cereal, flour and sugar in sealed containers.
Clean up spills and crumbs right away.
Keep a tight lid on the trash and empty it often.
Fix leaky faucets and dishwashers.
Seal cracks along baseboards, behind sinks and around pipes.
Clear out stacks of paper bags, newspapers and boxes.
